Use the gtrendsR package to collect data (use gtrendsR01.R program). Save the data into csv and R data formats. What are the differences between the two methods?

# install.packages("gtrendsR")
library(gtrendsR)

# Wait 10 seconds to avoid rate limiting
Sys.sleep(10)

# Query 5 years of trend data for all three terms
out <- gtrends(
  c("Trump", "Kamala Harris", "election"),
  onlyInterest = TRUE,
  geo = "US",
  gprop = "web",
  time = "today+5-y",
  category = 0
)

# Save the time series
df <- out$interest_over_time

# Plot the trends
plot(out)

# Another separate test query
Sys.sleep(10)
tg <- gtrends("tariff", time="all")


An advantage of the gtrendsR01 method is that the data is cleaner and organized better when the code is run; therefore, the plotting result is also cleaner, more visually appealing, and easier to read.


Due to repeated rate-limiting (429 status code errors) from the Google Trends API, the gtrendsR query would not render the plot in Quarto after too many times running the code. The original gtrendsR code is included for reproducibility. In place of the gtrends API plot, I downloaded the same Google Trends time-series data from online; this time frame shows the trends of these keywords over the past 12 months.

## Scraping Government data
## Website: GovInfo (https://www.govinfo.gov/app/search/)
## Prerequisite: Download from website the list of files to be downloaded

# install.packages(c("purrr", "magrittr")
library(purrr)
library(magrittr) # Alternatively, load tidyverse

## Set path for reading the listing and home directory
## For Windows, use "c:\\directory\\subdirectory\\"
## For Mac, "/Users/YOURNAME/path/"

save_dir <- "govdocs/"
library(rjson)
library(jsonlite)
library(data.table)
library(readr)

## CSV method
govfiles= read.csv(file="https://github.com/datageneration/datamethods/raw/refs/heads/master/webdata/govinfo-search-results-2024-10-13T07_10_42.csv", skip=2)

## JSON method
### rjson
gf_list <- rjson::fromJSON(file ="https://github.com/datageneration/datamethods/raw/refs/heads/master/webdata/govinfo-search-results-2024-10-13T07_18_29.json")
govfile2=dplyr::bind_rows(gf_list$resultSet)

### jsonlite
gf_list1 = jsonlite::read_json("https://github.com/datageneration/datamethods/raw/refs/heads/master/webdata/govinfo-search-results-2024-10-13T07_18_29.json")

### Extract the list
govfiles3 <- gf_list1$resultSet

### One more step
govfiles3 <- gf_list1$resultSet |> dplyr::bind_rows()


# Preparing for bulk download of government documents
govfiles$id = govfiles$packageId
pdf_govfiles_url = govfiles3$pdfLink
pdf_govfiles_id <- govfiles3$index

# Directory to save the pdf's
# Create a folder for storing the pdf's
# save_dir <- "govdocs/"

# Function to download pdfs
download_govfiles_pdf <- function(url, id) {
  tryCatch({
    destfile <- paste0(save_dir, "govfiles_", id, ".pdf")
    download.file(url, destfile = destfile, mode = "wb") # Binary files
    Sys.sleep(runif(1, 1, 3))  # Important: random sleep between 1 and 3 seconds to avoid suspicion of "hacking" the server
    return(paste("Successfully downloaded:", url))
  },
  error = function(e) {
    return(paste("Failed to download:", url))
  })
}

# Download files, potentially in parallel for speed
# Simple timer, can use package like tictoc

## Try downloading one document
start.time <- Sys.time()
message("Starting downloads")
results <- 1:1 %>% 
  purrr::map_chr(~ download_govfiles_pdf(pdf_govfiles_url[.], pdf_govfiles_id[.]))
message("Finished downloads")
end.time <- Sys.time()
time.taken <- end.time - start.time
time.taken

Time difference of 1.703185 secs

# Print results
print(results)

[1] "Successfully downloaded: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/BILLS-118sres890is/pdf/BILLS-118sres890is.pdf"

## Download 10 documents: 
start.time <- Sys.time()
message("Starting downloads")
results <- 1:10 %>%
  purrr::map_chr(~ download_govfiles_pdf(pdf_govfiles_url[.], pdf_govfiles_id[.]))
message("Finished downloads")
end.time <- Sys.time()
time.taken <- end.time - start.time
time.taken

Time difference of 21.43629 secs



Scraping documents from GovInfo can be difficult because the site structures its search results across multiple formats (CSV, JSON, XML), and each format organizes metadata differently. Another challenge is that some documents do not have direct PDF links, or their links may lead to redirected pages, which can cause errors in downloading the files. Additionally, government websites sometimes try to prevent automated downloads, so the script has to incorporate pauses (Sys.sleep) to avoid being blocked. One challenge pertaining to the code is that the R script requires a valid local directory (save_dir) to save the PDFs. If the folder does not exist or the path is incorrect, R gives an error or saves nothing. On macOS especially, missing slashes (“/”) or quotation issues can cause the script to fail.


The scraped PDFs are usable but not immediately ready for analysis. Because they are scanned government documents, many contain mixed formatting, non-text portions, inconsistent structure across documents, and more. All of these facors make it difficult to automatically extract clean text for text mining without additional processing steps. The metadata (title, date, committee, etc.) is usable, but the content itself needs preprocessing if the goal is text analytics.

Write a critique on a chart in a published work (book/article/news website).



Chart of Total Welfare Spending


This graph is supposed to depict the welfare spending per day and per hour on every household in poverty. This graph was used in a political argument by Republican senator Jeff Sessions. There are several reasons why this graph is misleading and doesn’t serve as an accurate visualization of the data.
Firstly, the chart excludes a large amount of context; there is no visible information about what types of welfare programs are being included or excluded from these statistics. The news article states that when doing the calculations for this chart, Sessions and his team included a wide variety of programs, including Medicaid, food stamps, and several other means-tested programs aimed at those with low incomes; he even includes health benefits given through an employer. The calculations also did not take into account the fact that many individuals who are not in poverty also benefit from these programs, but they are not included in the data shown in the chart. By not strictly defining what constitutes a welfare program and by not including a significant portion of welfare recipients in these data, Sessions has inflated the figure of $168 per day of welfare spending for those in poverty. Another issue is the fact that the chart is also comparing the welfare spending to median income; however, the median income does not include health benefits given by an employer, while Sessions’ calculation of the welfare spending does factor in those health benefits. This is an inaccurate and misleading comparison, especially given the argument Sessions is making and the way the chart is constructed to show the two amounts side by side.
In addition, the chart only shows these two dollar amounts - welfare spending per day and per hour, as compared to the median income per day and per hour. All parts of the chart, including axes, labels, and the graphed data as well, are very elementary and basic. Even the subtitle includes the inaccurate comparison to median income.
While the chart is simple to look at, it doesn’t convey anything meaningful; we don’t know what is considered a welfare program for these data, we don’t know from which or from how many individuals this data was gathered, and we don’t know when this data was collected. Readers can not trust the message that this graph is presenting without having access to the full context of the data. Considering all of these factors, we can assert that this chart is misleading and doesn’t effectively visually represent the data.

Biden-Xi Summit

The hashtag co-occurrence network forms two major clusters. The central cluster, containing hashtags like #china, #biden, #xijinping, #america, #americans, #fentanyl, and #coronavirus, reflects tweets focused on U.S.–China relations, public health, and political tensions. A second cluster highlights human-rights concerns, with hashtags such as #uyghurs, #uyghurgenocide, #tibetans, and #humanrights, suggesting that some users framed the summit around China’s human-rights record. Smaller, more isolated tags such as #ccp, #us, and #taiwan indicate side conversations, while still being loosely connected to the broader geopolitical context.


The user-mention network is fragmented into small, loosely connected clusters. This indicates that discussion was not dominated by a single highly connected group but instead by multiple independent sub-communities. One cluster includes journalists and policy analysts (such as @politico, @nahaltoosi, @anderscorr) discussing diplomatic implications. Another cluster centers around NBA-related accounts (such as @eneskanter, @washwizards, @nba), hinting at conversations involving sports and human rights. Smaller branches like @foxbusiness → @morningsmaria reflect mentions within media commentary. Overall, the network shows decentralized discourse with several separate conversation spheres rather than one cohesive discussion.
































The first wordcloud highlights the dominant themes of early U.S. presidential rhetoric, taken from early inaugural speeches (≤1826). As evidenced by their size in the word cloud, words like government, public, nation, people, states, union, and peace appear most frequently, emphasizing foundational concerns of establishing national unity, governance, and public duty. Other prominent words - including rights, powers, commerce, constitution, and citizens - reflect a strong focus on institutional structure, civic responsibility, and national identity as the US as an independent republic was still developing and defining early values.


The comparison wordcloud reveals distinct rhetorical patterns between the two presidents, Obama and Trump. Obama’s speeches emphasize collective responsibility and aspirational themes, reflected in words like us, must, generation, work, journey, and enduring. His language focuses more on unity, progress, and shared national challenges. Trump’s speeches attempt to garner national pride and involve action-oriented messaging, shown through words such as thank, america, country, great, president, bring, dreams, and going. His rhetoric places stronger emphasis on nationalism, achievement, and forward momentum. Overall, Obama’s tone is more inclusive and reflective, while Trump’s is more assertive and rooted in nationalism.


In the lexincal dispersion plot, the term “american” appears consistently across presidential inaugural speeches, but with varying emphasis. Earlier speeches from the 1950s–1970s show sporadic use, while later speeches from Reagan through Biden display more frequent and dense mentions. This suggests an increasing rhetorical focus on national identity and appeals to “the American people” in modern presidencies. Trump’s two speeches show especially high and frequent usage, indicating an intensified emphasis on nationalistic language.


The keyness plot shows which words are significantly more characteristic of each president’s inaugural speech. This shows similar patterns as those in the comparison wordcloud, as discussed above.



What is Wordfish?

Wordfish is an unsupervised text analysis model used to measure the political position or ideology of documents based on the words they use. It works by counting how often each word appears in each document and finding patterns in those word frequencies. This tool is widely used in political science to analyze parliamentary speeches, manifestos, debates, budget speeches, and more.

title: Literature & Media Reviews
text:
“Dataframed” is a podcast hosted by DataCamp featuring renowned data scientists’ insights of latest data science developments. Pick one recent podcast epidsode, listen, and write a one-page review.

I listened to the DataCamp episode titled “#298 Data Storytelling Skills to Increase Your Impact with Kat Green”. In this episode, Kat Green discusses the valuable skill that is data storytelling and why it is important for data to tell a story in order to be communicated in the most impactful way.


A key point that she makes is that it’s crucial to know your audience and how they will best receive the data; for example, you will have to take different approaches to your data storytelling depending on whether you’re presenting to your colleagues at work, your friends and family, the new person who just started at the company you work at, or the general public. Her approach is to always start with the big picture of your story or the main message you want to get across - then, based on your audience, you can add in more technical detail as needed. For instance, you can include a large amount of tecnical detail and jargon if you’re presenting to your team of coworkers, but if you’re presenting to a wider audience made up of the general public, it’s best to avoid jargon and technical terms and to make the message easy to digest for a broad spectrum of people. Green herself uses what is called the “3 Act Framework” - what she also calls the “And, What, Therefore” framework. The first act “And” gives background and context to the problem or issue you are describing and explains why it’s important or relevant. The second act “What” explains what the root of the problem or question is that you want to examine and the methods you will use to do so. The final act “Therefore” is when you give solutions to the problem and drive your argument home with final conclusions.


Green also advocates for practicing storytelling often in order to build and improve this skill. She claims that she herself starts all her data stories in written form in order to have clarity in what her story is trying to achieve. When the host asks her what role dashboards play in data storytelling, Green states that dashboards, in her view, are for those who already understand and are very familiar with the data, so it doesn’t have the same impact as data storytelling, which aims to reach a broader audience.


At the end of the podcast, the host asks Greene what she is most excited about in the world of data stories, and she replies that these days she is looking to sociology for inspiration and learning. She posits that especially in today’s world, a sociological perspective in analyzing data is critical, and being able to recognize social trends or systemic-level issues in data is a skill on its own. Greene further highlights the value of these kinds of skills in an era in which of a lot of data tends to be manipulated or misused.

The map of median household income across by county reveals strong regional disparities in Texas, with the highest median household incomes concentrated in major metropolitan areas such as Austin, Dallas–Fort Worth, and the suburban counties surrounding Houston. In contrast, the Rio Grande Valley and many of the rural western counties show substantially lower incomes. The map reflects how economic activity clusters around large urban centers, where jobs in tech, healthcare, business, and education contribute to higher household incomes. Rural and border areas tend to face greater structural disadvantages, including lower access to high-wage industries, higher poverty rates, lower educational attainment, and greater reliance on agricultural or service-based economies.


The Gini Index results show that both the highest and lowest inequality levels occur primarily in small, rural counties rather than in major urban centers. Counties with low Gini values (such as Crockett, Dallam, and Armstrong) tend to have relatively uniform income levels, often because most residents earn similar wages in agriculture or local service sectors. In contrast, counties with high Gini values (such as Loving, Sherman, and Presidio) are also rural but have very small populations, where even a few high-income households can substantially raise inequality. Urban counties like Dallas, Harris, Travis, and Bexar do not appear in the top or bottom lists because their Gini values fall closer to the middle of the distribution, indicating that their large populations produce more stable, moderate inequality estimates. Overall, the Gini Index results reveal that extreme inequality values in Texas are driven more by county size and population structure than by urbanization or overall income levels.

In addition to the foreign reserves table, I scraped a second Wikipedia table that lists U.S. states and territories by population. This table contained structured columns for rank, state name, population, and percent change, which allowed straightforward cleaning. I removed formatting characters (commas and percent signs), converted character fields to numeric, and standardized the column names. The final cleaned dataset contains population data for all 50 states plus U.S. territories.


The first step in creating a solid data plan for acquiring web data is to define the research question and determine what information is needed; from there, the key web sources where the information is published should be identified - for example: Wikipedia, the World Bank, government sites, the IMF, and more. The next step is to evaluate data accessibility, or how the data is best accessed; this can include public API, HTML tables, downloadable CSV or Excel files, and more. If appropriate, it is crucial to develop a web scraping strategy and determine which methods and tools (rvest, httr, jsonlite, tidyverse) make more sense. After that, it’s important to clean and validate the data, including by handling missing values, removing non-data rows, converting to numeric formats, and more. Lastly, data should be stored responsibly, depending on the scale of the project.
